recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say which nearby value you start from, and the formula you then apply.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Choose the nearby exact point
steps.margin_note: First mark, and the whole choice of method sits here: name x = 64, Δx = 1 and f′(64) = 1/16. An examiner reads this line to see whether the nearest perfect square was found.
lines: Let f(x) = √x. Then f(x + Δx) ≈ f(x) + f′(x)·Δx
64 is the nearest perfect square to 65, and √64 = 8 exactly

recall.must_convey: That x = 64 is chosen because √64 = 8 is exact, Δx = 1, and f′(64) = 1/16.

steps.why: The method only works from a point where the function is already known exactly. 64 is the nearest perfect square to 65, so the estimate starts at 8 with no calculator, and Δx = 1 is small next to 64.
common_mistakes: Choosing x = 65 itself, which leaves the square root still unknown.
Using 64 as a perfect cube and taking f(x) = ∛x, which answers a different question.
steps.memory_tip: For a square root, find the nearest perfect square; for a cube root, the nearest perfect cube. Δx carries whatever is left over.

steps.label: Apply the approximation formula
steps.margin_note: Second mark. 1/16 = 0.0625 exactly, so this one needs no rounding at all. 65 is above 64, so the correction is added.

steps.why: f′(x)·Δx is the correction the tangent line at x = 64 predicts. The true value is 8.062258, so this estimate is high by about 0.00024 — the tangent sits slightly above the curve, so a square-root estimate of this kind is always a little large.
common_mistakes: Giving 8.06 when the working already provides four decimal places.
steps.memory_tip: New value ≈ old value + slope × step. The step keeps its sign, so an upward move adds.
